title: UTI Antibiotics and Alcohol: Macrobid, Bactrim, Cipro, Keflex
excerpt: Can you drink on antibiotics for a UTI? How alcohol interacts with nitrofurantoin, Bactrim, Cipro, cephalexin, and fosfomycin, how it affects your bladder, and when to see a doctor.
metaDescription: Can you drink on UTI antibiotics? How alcohol interacts with Macrobid, Bactrim, Cipro, Keflex and fosfomycin, how long to wait, and when to see a doctor.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** none of the antibiotics most often prescribed for a urinary tract infection (UTI) has a dangerous, well-established chemical reaction with a moderate amount of alcohol. Nitrofurantoin (Macrobid), cephalexin (Keflex), fosfomycin (Monurol), and ciprofloxacin (Cipro) are generally not thought to react with alcohol the way metronidazole does. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (Bactrim, Septra) is the one with a murkier record, with scattered reports of flushing-type reactions, so many pharmacists tell people to skip alcohol on it. The bigger problem isn't a chemical clash. It's that alcohol works against a bladder that is already inflamed: it makes you pee more, then leaves you dehydrated, it can irritate the bladder lining, and it stacks onto the nausea and dizziness these drugs can cause on their own.

**The quick rules:** Find your antibiotic in the table below. If it's Bactrim or Septra (see our [Bactrim and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/bactrim-and-alcohol)), the cautious choice is no alcohol until the course is done. If it's nitrofurantoin ([our Macrobid guide](/never-hungover/nitrofurantoin-and-alcohol)), cephalexin, or fosfomycin, a single light drink is unlikely to cause a reaction or stop the drug working, but most people with a UTI will feel better and recover faster if they wait until the course is finished and the symptoms are gone. If you have fever, chills, back or side pain, or vomiting, that may be a kidney infection, so don't drink at all and call your doctor today.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and label guidance. It is not a substitute for the doctor or pharmacist who prescribed your antibiotic and knows your health history. **Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before drinking if** you're not sure which antibiotic you were given, you take other medicines, you're pregnant, you have kidney or liver disease, or this is a repeat or complicated infection. **Get medical help the same day if** you develop fever, chills, pain in your back or side, nausea and vomiting, or blood in your urine, or if your symptoms aren't improving after two to three days on the antibiotic. **Get emergency help (call 911) if** you have trouble breathing, swelling of the face, lips, or throat, a spreading rash or blistering skin, confusion, or fainting.

## How Alcohol and UTI Antibiotics Interact: The Mechanism in Plain Words

When people worry about "antibiotics and alcohol," they're usually thinking of one specific problem: a handful of drugs block the enzyme that clears **acetaldehyde**, the toxic compound your liver makes when it breaks down alcohol. If that enzyme is blocked, acetaldehyde builds up and you get flushing, a pounding headache, nausea, vomiting, and a racing heart. Doctors call it a "disulfiram-like reaction," after the drug disulfiram (Antabuse), which does this on purpose.

The antibiotics best known for this are **metronidazole (Flagyl)** and **tinidazole**, and they are not standard UTI drugs. (We cover them in detail in our [metronidazole and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/metronidazole-and-alcohol).) The common UTI antibiotics mostly don't work this way. So for a UTI, the real interaction tends to come through three other routes:

1. **Overlapping side effects.** Many UTI antibiotics can cause nausea, stomach upset, headache, or dizziness. Alcohol causes all of those too. Even without any chemical reaction, the two together can make you feel noticeably worse.
2. **Extra work for the liver and gut.** Alcohol and some antibiotics are both handled by the liver, and both can irritate the stomach. For a healthy person on a short course, this is usually minor. For a heavy drinker or someone with liver disease, it matters more.
3. **Working against the bladder itself.** This is the part specific to UTIs, and it's covered in its own section below. Alcohol changes how much and how often you pee, and it can irritate a bladder that is already inflamed.

There's one more piece worth knowing: there is no good evidence that a moderate amount of alcohol stops most antibiotics from killing bacteria. The drug still reaches your urine and does its job. The risk is more practical: people who drink heavily are more likely to miss doses, vomit up a dose, or stop the course early because they feel rough. For more on that question, see our guide to [whether alcohol makes antibiotics less effective](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-make-antibiotics-less-effective).

## UTI Antibiotics and Alcohol: Drug-by-Drug Table

Here's a quick summary of the antibiotics most often used for UTIs. It's general information, not a substitute for your own prescription label.

| Antibiotic (common brand) | Direct reaction with alcohol? | What to watch for | General advice |
|---|---|---|---|
| Nitrofurantoin (Macrobid, Macrodantin) | No well-established reaction | Nausea, headache; take with food | Light drinking unlikely to react, but waiting is kinder to your stomach and bladder |
| Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (Bactrim, Septra) | Possible; reports of flushing-type reactions | Nausea, rash, sun sensitivity | Many pharmacists advise no alcohol during the course |
| Ciprofloxacin (Cipro) | No chemical reaction | Dizziness, nerve and tendon side effects; separate from antacids and dairy | Avoid drinking enough to feel dizzy or unsteady |
| Cephalexin (Keflex) | No known reaction | Diarrhea, stomach upset | Light drinking unlikely to react |
| Fosfomycin (Monurol) | No known reaction | Diarrhea, nausea, headache | Single dose; waiting a day or so is sensible |
| Amoxicillin-clavulanate (Augmentin) | No known reaction | Diarrhea, nausea | Light drinking unlikely to react |

The sections below go through each one, including the variants people search for most.

## Can You Drink on Nitrofurantoin (Macrobid)?

Nitrofurantoin is one of the most common first-choice drugs for a simple bladder infection. It's sold as Macrobid (taken twice a day) and Macrodantin, and a typical course for uncomplicated cystitis is about five days. It concentrates in the urine and does very little elsewhere in the body, which is part of why it's popular for UTIs.

**Is there a reaction with alcohol?** There's no well-established disulfiram-like reaction between nitrofurantoin and alcohol. A few older references mention one, but it isn't a consistent finding, and it's not a standard label warning in the US.

**Why you might still wait:**

- **Nausea is the most common side effect.** Nitrofurantoin is known for upsetting the stomach, which is why it's meant to be taken with food. Alcohol adds to that. A drink on an empty stomach while you're on Macrobid is a reliable recipe for feeling queasy.
- **Antacids can get in the way.** Antacids containing magnesium trisilicate can reduce how much nitrofurantoin your body absorbs. If you reach for an antacid after drinking, check the ingredients and ask a pharmacist about spacing. (Our [Tums and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/tums-and-alcohol) covers antacids after drinking more broadly.)
- **It turns urine dark yellow or brown.** That's a harmless, expected effect of the drug, but it can be alarming if you're also dehydrated from drinking and don't know why your urine looks so dark.

Nitrofurantoin has rare but serious side effects, mostly seen with long-term use, including lung reactions and liver injury. Stop taking it and call your doctor if you develop a new cough, chest pain, shortness of breath, yellow skin or eyes, or dark urine with pale stools that doesn't fit the expected color change.

**Bottom line for Macrobid:** a single light drink is unlikely to cause a reaction, but it's not doing your stomach or your bladder any favors. Most people will feel better waiting until the five days are up.

## Can You Drink on Bactrim (Sulfamethoxazole-Trimethoprim)?

Bactrim and Septra combine two drugs, sulfamethoxazole (a "sulfa" drug) and trimethoprim. A typical course for a simple bladder infection is about three days, though it's prescribed for longer for other infections.

**Is there a reaction with alcohol?** This is the UTI antibiotic with the most uncertainty. There are case reports of people having a disulfiram-like reaction (flushing, rapid heartbeat, nausea) after drinking on it. These reports are rare, the mechanism isn't firmly established, and many people drink on Bactrim with no reaction at all. But because the risk can't be ruled out, many pharmacists and drug references advise avoiding alcohol while taking it.

**Other reasons to be careful:**

- **Trimethoprim works against folate.** It interferes with how the body uses folate (a B vitamin). Heavy drinkers often already run low on folate, so the combination is a particular concern for people who drink a lot on a regular basis.
- **It can raise potassium.** Trimethoprim can push blood potassium up, especially in older adults, people with kidney problems, or people taking certain blood pressure medicines. This isn't caused by alcohol, but it's one reason to tell your prescriber about every medicine you take.
- **Sulfa drugs can cause skin reactions and sun sensitivity.** A rash on Bactrim is a reason to call your doctor. A widespread rash with blisters, peeling, or mouth sores is an emergency.

**Bottom line for Bactrim:** this is the one where "skip the alcohol until you're done" is the clear advice. The course is usually short, so the wait is short too.

## Cipro and Alcohol for a UTI

Ciprofloxacin (Cipro) belongs to a family called fluoroquinolones, which also includes levofloxacin. It's still prescribed for some UTIs, especially kidney infections or when other drugs aren't suitable. The FDA has advised since 2016 that fluoroquinolones generally shouldn't be used for uncomplicated bladder infections when other options exist, because of the risk of serious side effects involving tendons, nerves, and the brain.

**Is there a reaction with alcohol?** No. Cipro doesn't cause a disulfiram-like reaction. But alcohol can add to the dizziness, light-headedness, and confusion that fluoroquinolones occasionally cause, and that can make falls or accidents more likely. Two other practical points:

- **Separate it from antacids, calcium, and dairy.** Minerals like calcium, magnesium, aluminum, iron, and zinc bind to ciprofloxacin and reduce how much you absorb. Taking a hangover antacid or a mineral-heavy electrolyte product at the same time as your dose can blunt it. Your label will say how many hours to leave between them.
- **Watch the caffeine.** Cipro can slow how your body clears caffeine, so the morning-after coffee may hit harder than usual and make jitters or a racing heart worse.

Stop the drug and call your doctor if you notice tendon pain (especially in the back of the heel), tingling or numbness in your hands or feet, or unusual mood changes. We go deeper in our [ciprofloxacin and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/ciprofloxacin-and-alcohol).

## Cephalexin (Keflex) and Alcohol

Cephalexin is a cephalosporin, a cousin of penicillin. It's often used for UTIs during pregnancy or when other drugs can't be used.

**Is there a reaction with alcohol?** No known reaction. You may read online that "cephalosporins cause a reaction with alcohol." That's true of a few specific ones, such as cefotetan, which have a particular chemical side chain and are mostly given in hospitals by injection. Cephalexin doesn't have that structure and isn't known to react with alcohol.

**What to watch for:** cephalexin's common side effects are diarrhea, nausea, and stomach upset, and alcohol can make those worse. Severe or bloody diarrhea during or after any antibiotic course is a reason to call your doctor, because it can signal a gut infection called C. difficile.

The same general picture applies to amoxicillin-clavulanate (Augmentin), another option for some UTIs: no known chemical reaction, but stomach side effects that alcohol can aggravate. See our [amoxicillin and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/amoxicillin-and-alcohol) for more.

## Fosfomycin (Monurol) and Alcohol

Fosfomycin is a single-dose treatment: a sachet of powder mixed into water and taken once. Because it's one dose, people often ask whether they can drink the same night.

**Is there a reaction with alcohol?** No known chemical reaction. The drug keeps working in the urine for a couple of days after that single dose, though, and its common side effects are diarrhea, nausea, and headache. Drinking that evening isn't known to be dangerous, but it's a strange time to add a bladder irritant and a diuretic. Waiting a day or two, until your symptoms ease, is the sensible move.

## Pivmecillinam, Azo, and Other UTI Medicines

A few other UTI medicines come up often:

- **Pivmecillinam (Pivya)**, approved in the US in 2024 for uncomplicated UTIs and used for years in Europe, is a penicillin-type antibiotic. It isn't known to have a chemical reaction with alcohol, but follow your label and pharmacist's advice.
- **Phenazopyridine (Azo, Pyridium)** isn't an antibiotic. It numbs the bladder to ease burning and turns urine bright orange. It doesn't treat the infection, so it shouldn't be used instead of seeing a doctor, and it's usually meant for only a couple of days. It isn't known to have a major interaction with alcohol, but because it can mask how bad your symptoms are, it can also hide the fact that a drink is making things worse.
- **Methenamine (Hiprex)** is used to prevent repeat UTIs rather than treat an active one. Ask your pharmacist about alcohol and any other medicines, since it relies on acidic urine to work.

## Does Alcohol Make a UTI Worse?

Even when there's no chemical reaction with your antibiotic, alcohol and an active UTI are a poor match. Here's why.

**Alcohol makes you pee more, then leaves you dry.** Alcohol suppresses vasopressin, the hormone that tells your kidneys to hold onto water. The result is more frequent urination while you drink, and often dehydration afterward. With a UTI, more frequent trips mean more of the burning and urgency you're already dealing with. Then the dehydration that follows makes urine more concentrated, which can sting more, and it means fewer trips to flush bacteria out. (Our guides on [why alcohol makes you pee](/never-hungover/why-does-alcohol-make-you-pee) and [whether alcohol dehydrates you](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-dehydrate-you) explain the hormone side of this.)

**Alcohol can irritate the bladder.** Alcohol, along with caffeine, carbonated drinks, and acidic drinks, shows up on most lists of common bladder irritants. That's based largely on what patients with bladder pain conditions report, rather than large trials, but plenty of people with a UTI notice that a drink makes the burning and urgency worse. Mixed drinks combine several of these at once: alcohol, fizz, citrus, and sometimes caffeine.

**Alcohol can blunt your immune response.** Heavy drinking is known to impair the immune system. One or two drinks won't undo your antibiotic, but a big night while your body is fighting an infection works against recovery. Alcohol also fragments sleep, and sleep matters when you're ill.

**It can hide a worsening infection.** A hangover and an early kidney infection can look alike at first: feeling achy, tired, nauseous, maybe sweaty. If you've been drinking, it's easier to shrug off a fever or back pain as "just a hangover." That's the scenario to watch out for.

### Can alcohol cause a UTI?

There's no good evidence that alcohol directly causes UTIs. UTIs are caused by bacteria, most often E. coli from the gut, reaching the urethra and bladder. But nights out can set up conditions that make one more likely: holding your urine for long stretches, being dehydrated, and having sex without peeing afterward. If you notice UTIs tend to follow nights of drinking, those habits are a more likely link than the alcohol itself.

## How Long After UTI Antibiotics Can You Drink?

For the common UTI antibiotics, there's no special waiting period the way there is for metronidazole (where labels usually say to wait at least three days after the last dose). A sensible approach is:

- **Finish the course as prescribed.** UTI symptoms often improve within a day or two, and it's tempting to celebrate early. Take every dose your doctor prescribed unless they tell you otherwise.
- **Wait until your symptoms are gone.** If you still have burning or urgency, alcohol is likely to make it feel worse.
- **For Bactrim, wait until the course is done.** Given the uncertainty about reactions, this is the cautious line. Some pharmacists suggest giving it an extra day.
- **For fosfomycin, give it a day or two.** The single dose keeps working in your urine for a while.
- **If your symptoms come back after the course, see your doctor before drinking.** A returning UTI may need a different antibiotic or a urine culture.

## Hidden Alcohol and Other Morning-After Mix-Ups

A few common combinations catch people out while they're on a UTI antibiotic:

- **Antacids and mineral supplements.** Calcium, magnesium, and aluminum antacids and many electrolyte or multivitamin products can reduce the absorption of ciprofloxacin and, for magnesium trisilicate, nitrofurantoin. If you use them after drinking, space them from your antibiotic dose as your label or pharmacist directs.
- **Painkillers.** Ibuprofen and naproxen are hard on the stomach and kidneys, especially when you're dehydrated. Acetaminophen has its own alcohol warning. See our [Tylenol and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) before combining it with a night out.
- **Cranberry products.** Cranberry is often suggested for UTIs. A 2023 Cochrane review found that cranberry products reduced the risk of repeat symptomatic UTIs in some groups, especially women with recurrent infections. That's prevention, not treatment. Cranberry juice won't cure an active infection, and a cranberry vodka is still a vodka.
- **Liquid medicines with alcohol.** Some liquid cold medicines contain alcohol. It's not usually an issue with these antibiotics, but it's worth knowing if you're on Bactrim and trying to avoid alcohol entirely.

## When to See a Doctor

Most bladder infections respond quickly to the right antibiotic. These signs mean something more is going on.

**Call your doctor the same day if:**

- You have **fever, chills, or shaking**
- You have **pain in your back, side, or flank** (just below the ribs)
- You have **nausea or vomiting**, especially if you can't keep your antibiotic down
- You see **blood in your urine** that's new or getting worse
- Your symptoms **aren't improving after two to three days** on the antibiotic, or they come back soon after finishing
- You're **pregnant**, **male**, have **diabetes**, a **weakened immune system**, or a **urinary catheter** (UTIs in these groups are treated as more complicated)
- You develop a **rash**, severe diarrhea, tendon pain, or numbness or tingling while on the antibiotic

**Go to the emergency room or call 911 if:**

- You have **trouble breathing** or swelling of the face, lips, or throat
- You have a **spreading rash, blisters, or peeling skin**
- You have a **high fever with confusion**, a racing heart, or feel faint, which can be signs the infection has spread to the blood

Fever and back pain after a night out are easy to blame on a hangover. If they come with a UTI, assume it's the infection until a doctor tells you otherwise.

## Who Should Be Most Careful

You should talk to your doctor or pharmacist before having any alcohol on a UTI antibiotic if you:

- Are **pregnant or trying to get pregnant** (alcohol isn't recommended in pregnancy regardless of antibiotics)
- Have **kidney disease**, which affects how several UTI antibiotics are dosed
- Have **liver disease** or drink heavily on a regular basis
- Are **older** or take blood pressure medicines that raise potassium (relevant for Bactrim)
- Take **blood thinners such as warfarin**, since several antibiotics, Bactrim and Cipro included, can change how warfarin works
- Have had a **reaction to a sulfa drug** before

## A Note on Hangover Supplements While You're on Antibiotics

If you're searching this because you have a wedding or a trip coming up mid-course, the simplest plan is the one that works: drink lightly or not at all, alternate with water, eat, and pee when you need to rather than holding it.

Some people use DHM (dihydromyricetin), a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism, before a night out. To be clear about where it stands: there is no good evidence about DHM combined with antibiotics, there's no evidence it changes how any UTI antibiotic works, and it does nothing for an infection. It also doesn't make it safe to drink on Bactrim or any other medicine your pharmacist told you to avoid alcohol with. If you're on a course, ask your pharmacist before adding any supplement. Once you've finished treatment and feel well, and you want to try it for future nights out, a well-reviewed, budget-friendly option is [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when, and our broader [antibiotics and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/antibiotics-and-alcohol) covers drugs beyond UTIs.

## The Bottom Line

- The common UTI antibiotics (nitrofurantoin, cephalexin, fosfomycin, ciprofloxacin) aren't known to cause a dangerous chemical reaction with a moderate amount of alcohol.
- **Bactrim and Septra** are the exception worth respecting: there are reports of flushing-type reactions, so the cautious advice is no alcohol during the course.
- Even without a reaction, alcohol works against a UTI by making you pee more, then dehydrating you, irritating the bladder, and adding to nausea and dizziness.
- Separate antacids and mineral supplements from ciprofloxacin and nitrofurantoin doses.
- Finish the course, wait until symptoms are gone, then drink if you want to.
- Fever, chills, back or side pain, or vomiting with a UTI may be a kidney infection. Don't drink, and call your doctor today.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking antibiotics for a UTI?**

For most common UTI antibiotics, including nitrofurantoin (Macrobid), cephalexin (Keflex), fosfomycin (Monurol), and ciprofloxacin (Cipro), a single light drink is not known to cause a dangerous reaction or stop the drug working. Bactrim (sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim) is the exception, with reports of flushing-type reactions, so many pharmacists advise no alcohol on it. Even when there's no reaction, alcohol can make UTI burning and urgency worse, so waiting until the course is done and symptoms are gone is the better choice. Ask your pharmacist if you're unsure.

**Can I drink alcohol on nitrofurantoin (Macrobid)?**

There is no well-established chemical reaction between nitrofurantoin and alcohol. But nitrofurantoin commonly causes nausea and is meant to be taken with food, and alcohol adds to stomach upset. Some antacids containing magnesium trisilicate can also reduce absorption of nitrofurantoin. A light drink is unlikely to cause a reaction, but most people feel better waiting until the roughly five-day course is finished.

**Can you drink on Bactrim for a UTI?**

It's best not to. There are case reports of disulfiram-like reactions, with flushing, rapid heartbeat, and nausea, in people who drank while taking sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim. They are rare and not fully explained, but because the risk can't be ruled out, many pharmacists and drug references advise avoiding alcohol during the course. Trimethoprim also interferes with folate, which is a particular concern for heavy drinkers.

**Does alcohol make a UTI worse?**

It can. Alcohol suppresses the hormone that helps your kidneys hold water, so you pee more often while drinking and are often dehydrated afterward, which concentrates your urine. Alcohol is also listed as a common bladder irritant, and heavy drinking can blunt your immune response and disrupt sleep. There's no good evidence that a moderate drink stops your antibiotic working, but it often makes the symptoms feel worse.

**How long after UTI antibiotics can I drink alcohol?**

For nitrofurantoin, cephalexin, fosfomycin, and ciprofloxacin there's no special waiting period like the three days usually advised after metronidazole. A sensible approach is to finish the full course and wait until your symptoms are gone. For Bactrim, wait until the course is complete. For single-dose fosfomycin, giving it a day or two is sensible because the drug keeps working in your urine for a while.

**Can I drink alcohol on cephalexin for a UTI?**

Cephalexin (Keflex) isn't known to cause a reaction with alcohol. The cephalosporins linked to alcohol reactions, such as cefotetan, have a specific chemical structure that cephalexin doesn't share and are mostly given in hospitals. Cephalexin can cause diarrhea and stomach upset, which alcohol can make worse. Severe or bloody diarrhea on any antibiotic is a reason to call your doctor.

**Can alcohol cause a UTI?**

There's no good evidence that alcohol directly causes UTIs, which are caused by bacteria reaching the bladder. But nights out can set up conditions that make one more likely, such as holding your urine for long periods, being dehydrated, and having sex without urinating afterward. If your UTIs tend to follow nights of drinking, those habits are the more likely link.

**When should I see a doctor about a UTI?**

Call your doctor the same day if you have fever, chills, pain in your back or side, nausea or vomiting, new blood in your urine, or no improvement after two to three days on the antibiotic, since these can signal a kidney infection or a drug that isn't working. Go to the emergency room if you have trouble breathing, facial swelling, a blistering rash, or a high fever with confusion. Don't drink alcohol if you have any of these symptoms.
